quote: Beweise, dass es ein System von Gl. $f_1(x_1 .. x_n) = 0$, $f_2(x_1 .. x_n) = 0$, .. giebt, so dass alle durch die ersten Gl. dargestellten $x_1 .. x_n$ die letzten Gl. befriedigen und auch die letzten Gl. nur durch jene Wertsysteme befriedigt werden.
english: Prove that there is a system of equations $f_1(x_1..x_n)=0$, $f_2(x_1..x_n)=0$, ..., such that all $x_1..x_n$ represented by the first equations satisfy the latter equations, and the latter equations are satisfied only by those systems of values.
topic: The page ends a remark that function theory draws its strength from its border with number theory and should follow arithmetic, gives an aphorism about the heights of arithmetic, and then sets a problem with a proof sketch: show that points given by homogeneous parametrizations $x_i=\varphi_i(t_1,\dots,t_\nu)$ are exactly the solutions of a system of homogeneous equations.

triage.modern_statement: Let φ_1,…,φ_n be homogeneous polynomials (forms) of the same degree in t_1,…,t_ν. Show that the set of points x = (φ_1(t):…:φ_n(t)) is exactly the zero set of finitely many homogeneous polynomials f_j(x_1,…,x_n). That means the image of the map P^{ν-1} → P^{n-1} is a projective algebraic variety: the parametrized set can be described implicitly, with no extra solutions. In modern terms this is the implicitization problem together with the closedness of images of projective morphisms. Exact equality, rather than equality only up to Zariski closure, holds over an algebraically closed field when the φ_i have no common nontrivial zero. A finite system of equations always exists by Hilbert's basis theorem.
triage.answered_by: This is classical elimination theory: resultants (Kronecker and others in the 19th century), Hilbert's own basis theorem and Nullstellensatz (1890/1893), and later the 'main theorem of elimination theory' (the image of a projective variety under a projection is a variety; in scheme language, projective schemes are proper). Effective implicitization by Gröbner bases was worked out from the 1980s–90s, for example in the 1992 Journal of Symbolic Computation paper 'Implicitization of rational parametric equations'. For general affine or rational maps the image is only constructible (Chevalley's theorem), so one obtains the closure.

evidence.claim: Main theorem of elimination theory: every projective scheme is proper, so the image of a projective variety under a projection is again a variety. A version of this predates schemes.
Wikidata describes the theorem as: image of a projective variety by a projection is also a variety.
Sturmfels' notes on elimination and implicitization: the Zariski closure of the image of a variety under a polynomial map is a variety, and its ideal is computed by elimination (I ∩ K[x]).
Gröbner basis algorithms give a complete solution for finding a basis of the implicit prime ideal of rational parametric equations.
For maps between affine varieties the image is generally only constructible (Chevalley), so locally closed approximations or closures are needed.

triage.why: The note asks whether a homogeneously parametrized set equals the solution set of a system of homogeneous equations. That is the implicitization / elimination question, and it was settled by classical elimination theory and by Hilbert's own basis theorem. The modern statement is the main theorem of elimination theory, with exact equality when the parametrization has no base points over an algebraically closed field; otherwise the result holds for the Zariski closure. The note is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. Algorithmic implicitization is still studied in computational algebra, but the existence question itself is not open. Confidence is medium for two reasons. The note's exact intended hypotheses (field, base points) are unclear. And none of the sources found ties this diary entry to a specific later publication.
